stops.name: New York, the Chanin Theatre: thunder on Broadway
stops.campa: Sol Hurok brings her across the ocean, and in the last days of December 1930 the curtain of the Chanin Theatre rises on a solitary German woman who dances to a gong and a drum. The house is sold out; the applause comes down like weather, a welcome she will carry to her deathbed. Depression America, which knows Denishawn's silks, has never seen this: space itself made adversary and partner. Martha Graham's generation is in the seats. Over three seasons she gives one hundred seventy performances across the continent, and modern dance becomes a two-shored art.

stops.name: New York, the Wigman School of Hanya Holm
stops.campa: The mission plants its American house: the New York Wigman School opens under Hanya Holm, the quiet, exact apostle sent from the Dresden mother-house. Through her the doctrine of breath, swing and space enters the bloodstream of American dance: Holm will Americanize the school under her own name when the German name grows heavy, and her line runs on through Bessie Schönberg and Alwin Nikolais into everything after. The canon counts this storefront of studios among Wigman's most durable works: a school begotten of a school, begetting schools.

stops.name: Dresden, the Gleichschaltung reaches the hill-house
stops.campa: The new masters of Germany take the culture into their fist, and the priestess of the absolute dance does not emigrate. She takes the local leadership of the dance section in the regime's teachers' league; she signs what is put before her; Jewish pupils and colleagues vanish from the rolls of the school and from the record of the art. The canon does not look away: she wagers that the German dance can ride the German state, and pays for the wager in every register: first with her conscience's company, later with the school itself.

stops.name: Berlin, the German Dance Festival of the new state
stops.campa: At the German Dance Festival mounted under the Reich Culture Chamber in Berlin, Ausdruckstanz performs before the state that claims it as a national art. Wigman dances her women's dances; the halls are full; the ministries smile. It is the honeymoon of a marriage the canon already knows to be a devouring: the regime wants festival bodies and folk choirs, not daimons and witches, and the smile of official favor is the same fixed smile as the witch-mask's. Each season after this one, the freedom of the hill-house narrows by a degree.

stops.name: Berlin, the Olympic Stadium: Totenklage before the hundred thousand
stops.campa: On the opening night of the Olympiad, in the festival play Olympische Jugend, Wigman leads eighty dancers in Totenklage, the lament for the dead, to Werner Egk's music, under the flame, before a hundred thousand in the Berlin stadium and the cameras of the world. It is the movement choir's greatest and last cathedral. She has refused to make the triumphal piece wanted of her; she gives the Games mourning instead, women grieving for the fallen at the feast of the nations that are three years from falling on each other. The regime does not forgive the gift.

stops.name: Dresden, the long disfavor
stops.campa: After the Games the cold sets in. The subsidies thin, the invitations lapse, the ministry's word for her art hardens toward the vocabulary it uses for the condemned painters. She dances the Herbstliche Tänze, the autumnal dances, a title the canon hears as plain speech, and holds the school together year by year as the war comes and takes the students, the coal, the light. Her companion of the Nazi years, an industrialist bound to the armaments state, is pressed apart from her. The regime that embraced the German dance is strangling it with the same arms.

stops.name: Dresden, the school sold, the farewell danced
stops.campa: On 1 April 1942 the hill-house passes from her hands: the Wigman school is sold and swallowed as a department of the Dresden conservatory. That year, at the Komödienhaus, the fifty-five-year-old dances her last solo evening and names it what it is: Abschied und Dank, farewell and thanks. The woman who entered as the witch goes out as the guest thanking the house. Twenty-two years of the Dresden temple end in an inventory and a bow. She leaves for Leipzig, a teacher without a school, carrying the language in her body like contraband.

stops.name: Leipzig, teaching under the bombs
stops.campa: In Leipzig, where her sister Elisabeth had kept a school before her, she teaches dance at the Musikhochschule while the air war dismantles the city around the lessons. The studio work goes on between alarms: breath, swing, fall, recovery; the curriculum now indistinguishable from instructions for surviving. The pupils are girls of the catastrophe; she is their proof that the art has outlived one German collapse already and intends to outlive another. In the nights she writes, and waits, one more winter resident in the long sanatorium that Germany has become.

stops.name: Leipzig, the night Dresden burns
stops.campa: On the night of 13 February 1945 the firestorm takes Dresden. Word and, the tradition says, the glow on the horizon reaches Leipzig, and Wigman keeps vigil for the city of her ascension: the guild-hall of the first triumph, the Postplatz rooms, the theatres, the streets her pupils crossed for twenty years, burning in one night. The hill-house on the Bautzner Strasse survives above the ruin like a relic. The canon sets this among her death-dances: Totenmal was danced for the last war's dead, and the new dead now outnumber every choir.

stops.name: Leipzig, professor at sixty
stops.campa: The war ends and she is still standing, sixty years old in the Soviet zone, and she builds again: at the reopened Hochschule she heads the dance department and installs a four-semester training; on her sixtieth birthday the new order names her professor. In the spring she petitions for a central academy of dance for the whole of Germany: the old dream of the dancers' congresses, filed now with commissars. She choreographs, teaches, examines: the daimon in a professor's chair, conducting the language of dance through the rubble semester by semester.

stops.name: Leipzig, Orpheus again: the ring closes on Hellerau
stops.campa: For the Leipzig opera she choreographs Gluck's Orpheus und Eurydike: the very work through which, as a mutinous pupil at Hellerau thirty-five years before, she first felt dance chafing in the service of music. Now the servant returns as master of the rite: her Orpheus descends among the shades in a Germany that is itself an underworld, and the plea to lead the beloved dead back into the light is understood by every soul in the house. The canon loves such rings; it marks this one and counts the years, 1912 to 1947, like beads.

stops.name: Berlin-Dahlem, the flight west and the third founding
stops.campa: In the spring of 1949 the state nationalizes her Leipzig work out from under her, and on the fourth of July she crosses to West Berlin, sixty-two years old, founding for the third time. In a villa on the Rheinbabenallee in Dahlem she opens the Mary Wigman-Studio with Marianne Vogelsang: bare floor, drum, gong, the whole apparatus of the language reassembled once more. To this room come the postwar pilgrims from every continent; among the last of them, a quiet Japanese student named Kazuo Ohno's generation carries the seed onward into butoh's dark.
